newsitem.title: GERMANY: German February jobs data seen better than expected.
newsitem.headline: German February jobs data seen better than expected.

text.p: German politicians on Monday knocked down news reports that unemployment hit a record 4.8 million last month as the country's deep jobs crisis threatens to derail efforts to join Europe's single currency.

Unemployment has recently set records from month to month, reaching levels not seen since the turbulent 1930s and forcing Bonn's political parties to try to abandon differences to reach consensus on measures to boost private investment and jobs.

Mastering the jobs crisis could make or break re-election prospects for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 14-year-old coalition next year, while the high costs of unemployment could spoil Bonn's efforts to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda, in an interview with Monday's Bild daily, dismissed the figure, but warned of social unrest unless Bonn gets the upper hand on joblessness.
There were a total of 4.66 million Germans out of work in January. Sunday's Bild am Sonntag reported that February unemployment surged to 4.8 million.
"I cannot confirm this number and I consider it unlikely," said Jagoda. "But I fear that one day there will be a rude awakening if we do not get a handle on unemployment soon."
Jobless figures for February will be published on Thursday.

The Federal Statistics Office will release gross domestic product (GDP) data for the fourth quarter and 1996 on Wednesday and is expected to revise downward its previous 1996 growth number to 1.3 percent from a preliminary 1.4 percent.
Economists polled by Reuters on Monday forecast fourth quarter GDP fell around 0.2 percent from the third quarter but rose between 1.6 and 1.9 percent from a year earlier.
The reported rise in February jobless was widely disputed and independent economists even forecast that unemployment could have fallen on a seasonally-adjusted basis.
Speaking to reporters in Bergen, Norway, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said unemployment edged a little higher last month, but dismissed the report of a huge rise.
"I believe the number will rise only slightly in February, not the figure that was reported. It will be roughly the same as January, perhaps a bit more," he said.
The Federation of German Trade Unions (DGB), which has a seat on the board of the Labour Office, also said it was unlikely that unemployment rose as much as the reports said.
"There are no indications of such a figure," said DGB deputy president Ursula Engelen-Kefer.
If jobless numbers rose to 4.8 million in unadjusted terms, as reported by Bild, this would imply a rise of over 100,000 on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to economists.
"As a result of the mild weather, which was very important for the building sector, we expect a seasonally-adjusted decline of around 30,000," said Joerg Kraemer of Merrill Lynch.
Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, predicted a seasonally-adjusted fall of 40,000 "because of the good weather in February".
But Ulrike Kastens of Trinkaus Capital Management did not expect unemployment to fall, saying weak building orders offset any benefits of the mild weather conditions.
"The mood is just very, very bad," she said.
With its austerity drive to meet the tight budget deficit limit set out in the Maastricht treaty on EMU, Bonn has little room to boost jobs.
But Jagoda urged the government to introduce a programme to promote investment and force a turnaround on the labour market.
"It is essential now to promote more investment," he said. "A programme to boost investment could indeed stimulate job creation."

Heiner Flasbeck, chief economist of the DIW institute in Berlin, backed Jagoda's suggestion, urging the government to boost borrowing to finance such a programme and for the Bundesbank to make it affordable by lowering interest rates.
"In this way, according to the classical model, we could stimulate the economy and that would bring jobs," he said.

But, hoping still to make the grade for EMU, the government has all but ruled out any jobs programme that would require raising the budget deficit. Instead, it says the economy is on track and growth will bring jobs.
